intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple epiphyseal dysplasia-2 (EDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen (COL9A2) on chromosome 1p32.3-p33.

checks.claim: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia-2 (EDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the COL9A2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation screening of candidate regions revealed a novel point mutation at position -1 in the COL9A2 exon 3/intron 3 splicing region.
checks.explanation: The abstract links a COL9A2 mutation to EDM2 in this family, but it never says the mutation is heterozygous.

checks.claim: The COL9A2 gene encodes the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen.
checks.evidence_quote: The genes encoding alpha 2(IX) collagen (COL9A2) map to human chromosome 1p32.3-p33 and mouse chromosome 4.
checks.explanation: The title identifies COL9A2 as the gene encoding alpha 2(IX) collagen.

checks.claim: The COL9A2 gene is located on chromosome 1p32.3-p33.
checks.evidence_quote: COL9A2 was mapped to human chromosome 1p32.3-p33 using fluorescence in situ hybridization.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives this exact location.

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a dominantly inherited chondrodysplasia characterized by mild short stature and early-onset osteoarthrosis (Briggs et al., 1994). EDM2 is a subtype of MED in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age. Beginning in childhood, the disease causes pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints, and affected individuals are prone to early degenerative joint disease (Fiedler et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Versteylen et al. (1988) described 2 families that appeared to have multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. In both families, severe osteochondritis of the knees was strikingly common. The authors suggested that the fragmented and maldeveloped epiphyses characteristic of epiphyseal dysplasia caused the osteochondritis.

paragraphs.text: Fiedler et al. (2002) reported a family of 19 individuals over 4 generations, 12 of whom were affected with a variant of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Beginning in childhood, the disease caused pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints. Some adult patients had repeated episodes of free articular bodies that caused the joint to lock, and affected individuals were prone to early degenerative joint disease. The hips were not markedly affected at an early age. On electron microscopy, the diameter of collagen fibrils from free articular bodies removed arthroscopically from 2 patients did not differ obviously from that of normal articular cartilage.

paragraphs.text: Briggs et al. (1994) performed linkage studies in a large family with MED. They excluded the chromosome 19 interval to which both pseudoachondroplasia and a form of MED had previously been linked. Instead, they identified an MED locus, EDM2, on the short arm of chromosome 1 (1p32.2-33), in a region containing the COL9A2 gene, which encodes the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen.

paragraphs.text: Fiedler et al. (2002) screened candidate regions in a 4-generation family with EDM2 and identified a G-to-C substitution at position -1 in the COL9A2 exon 3/intron 3 splicing region. They predicted that the change most probably alters splicing. Using automated sequencing and BsaWI digestion of amplicons, they confirmed the substitution in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 presymptomatic young children. Fiedler et al. (2002) concluded, together with previous reports, that mutations causing skipping of exon 3 within the COL3 domain of the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen may be relatively common in patients with an MED subtype in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age.
